analysis.one_liner: Tightens pipeline safety rules, requires public disclosure of pipeline risks, and lets citizens sue pipeline operators.
analysis.headline: Senator Markey's pipeline safety and transparency bill received no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote before Congress ended, dying in the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force pipeline operators to install automatic shutoff valves that stop a rupture within 30 minutes in populated areas, write the first federal safety rules for carbon dioxide pipelines, and block hydrogen blending in home gas lines until Congress passes safety rules. It would require operators to publish — and mail to nearby residents — what's flowing through pipelines, where they run, and what their incident history is. It would also strip industry financial conflicts from federal safety advisory committees, let citizens sue operators that violate safety law, raise penalties, and extend a federal grant program to help gas utilities repair, replace, or retire leaky local pipelines.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school near gas, hazardous liquid, and carbon dioxide pipelines — especially in densely populated and environmental justice communities — would get rupture-shutoff requirements, first-time safety rules for carbon dioxide pipelines, and annual notices about the pipelines near them. Residents could request detailed safety data about any pipeline, including pressure limits, incident history, and rupture modeling. Local first responders would get carbon dioxide rupture training. Workers on grant-funded gas projects would get prevailing-wage preference. Taxpayers and regulators would gain better incident reporting, and citizens would gain the right to sue violators.

how_it_helps.text: Operators of gas, hazardous liquid, and carbon dioxide pipelines in high-consequence areas would have to fully isolate a ruptured segment within 30 minutes, and within 5 years prove they can do so, dramatically cutting the volume of fuel released in a rupture.

The bill would require the first federal minimum safety standards for carbon dioxide pipelines, including leak detection, fracture protection, and emergency responder training, responding to a 2022 pipeline rupture in Satartia, Mississippi that hospitalized dozens.

Operators would have to publish pipeline contents, valve locations, incident history, rupture zones, and decommissioning plans on free public websites, and annually notify owners, tenants, and first responders near pipelines of the risks and their legal rights.
Federal technical safety committee members would be barred from having financial interests in pipeline, petroleum, ethanol, or gas industries and would have to disclose their finances annually.

Citizens could bring civil suits for penalties and injunctions against pipeline safety violations and against the Transportation Secretary for failing to perform mandatory duties, and penalties for a related series of violations would no longer be capped.

Regulators would have to consider climate impacts and whether a project unnecessarily prolongs fossil fuel infrastructure when writing pipeline standards, and a GAO study would examine the safety and climate risks of blending hydrogen into home gas lines, with a ban on such blending until Congress provides a regulatory framework.

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline operators and natural gas utilities would bear the costs: retrofitting rupture-mitigation valves, building carbon dioxide pipeline safety programs, publishing safety data, and defending citizen lawsuits. Federal taxpayers would fund $200 million per year in gas distribution grants plus a $12 million-per-year public engagement office. Gas customers could see some compliance costs passed through utility rates, and hydrogen blending bans could delay a pathway some utilities hoped to use to reduce emissions.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for valve retrofits, disclosure systems, and carbon dioxide safety programs would be substantial for pipeline operators, and gas utilities could pass some of these costs to customers through rates.

The outright ban on hydrogen blending in existing gas distribution lines, even at low percentages, forecloses a possible emissions-reduction pathway until Congress acts, which some energy analysts consider overly rigid given unresolved safety questions the bill itself would study.

The bill extends rather than redirects the gas distribution grant program, spending up to $1 billion more with only 20 percent reserved for non-emitting alternatives, so most funds could still repair or replace fossil gas pipes.

A broader citizen right to sue could produce litigation volume and expense that slows compliance, and the 30-minute isolation mandate includes a waiver process that could dilute the requirement for operators who claim infeasibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety and transparency gains for the millions of Americans who live near large pipelines are real and concrete: faster rupture shutoffs, first-ever carbon dioxide pipeline rules, and mailed risk notices. The costs fall mainly on the regulated industry, though some will reach gas customers' bills. The bill's weakest points are its rigid hydrogen-blending ban and the fact that most of its new grant money still flows to fossil gas infrastructure. On balance, it is a well-aimed safety and accountability bill with some design choices that could be debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on August 1, 2024, near the end of a session, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor in the Senate.
No further action was taken after the committee referral; no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline operators, gas utilities, and other fossil fuel interests are better off because the bill died, avoiding rupture-valve retrofits, public safety-data disclosure, an expanded citizen right to sue, and climate considerations in pipeline regulation. Members of Congress avoided taking a recorded position on any of it.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; he had no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (and its Chair)
against.role: Committee where the bill was referred and died
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to expire at the end of the 118th Congress without action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so no partisan split is recorded; the only on-record sponsor was a Democrat and it drew zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and hazardous liquid pipeline operators
industries.note: The bill would impose 30-minute rupture isolation requirements in populated areas, extensive public disclosure of pipeline contents, locations, and incident histories, broader citizen lawsuits, and uncapped penalties for a series of violations. Their financial interest in avoiding these mandates runs directly against the safety interests of nearby residents.

Utilities would face hydrogen-blending bans and reporting duties, but the bill authorizes $200 million per year of federal grants they could use to repair, replace, or retire local gas pipelines — with at least 20 percent reserved for non-emitting alternatives. Most grant money could still subsidize fossil gas pipes, partly entrenching their infrastructure while funding upgrades.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and carbon dioxide pipeline developers
industries.note: The bill would impose the first federal safety standards, odorization, geohazard assessment, and public rupture-zone disclosure on carbon dioxide pipelines, adding compliance costs to an industry seeking to scale up. Its interest in operating without these rules runs against communities in potential rupture zones.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel interests on federal safety advisory committees
industries.note: Industry-aligned members of technical safety standards committees would be barred from holding financial interests in the pipeline, petroleum, ethanol, or gas industries. This removes a channel of industry influence over the standards that govern pipeline safety.
